title: Seeing Unseen Gravitational Wave Inspirals at the Galactic Center
comment: Accepted for publication ApJ Letters
summary: The Galactic Center is expected to host a population of extremely large mass-ratio inspirals (X-MRIs) migrating toward the supermassive black hole. We propose an observational approach utilizing the secular gravitational torque exerted by X-MRIs on the highly eccentric S-star S301. This approach is intrinsically limited by the stochastic nature of the surrounding stellar-mass black hole cusp. As S301 propagates through this granular medium, it experiences discrete gravitational encounters. Standard orbital fitting procedures inherently assume a smooth background potential; applying them to stochastic trajectories averages these discrete velocity discontinuities into a continuous secular drift. This introduces a systematic bias that mimics the X-MRI precession signal, invalidating traditional mass estimation techniques. To resolve this degeneracy, we implement a methodology based on the Wavelet Transform Modulus Maxima method to characterize the local Hölder regularity of the orbital motion. This model isolates the singular discontinuities induced by stellar-mass black hole encounters from the continuous torque of the X-MRI distribution, allowing for detection even when instantaneous accelerations are below the instrumental noise threshold. We demonstrate analytically that S301 is highly sensitive to the interior X-MRI population while remaining dynamically decoupled from the secular influence of the exterior cusp. Combining precision astrometry and radial velocity projections, we establish that a minimal population of two X-MRIs is detectable within a five to nine-year timeframe, allowing us to constrain the presence of an unseen orbiter population prior to the launch of space-based gravitational wave detectors.

title: Thinner Disks Struggle to Launch Jets: GRMHD Simulations of Magnetic Field Generation and Transport
comment: Submitted to MNRAS comments welcomed
summary: Relativistic jets are observed in some accreting black-hole systems but not others. In X-ray binaries, jet production is closely associated with geometrically thicker accretion states, suggesting that disk thickness may influence the conditions for jet launching. We investigate this connection using three-dimensional GRMHD simulations of disks with $h/r=0.1$--$0.3$, initialized with a toroidal magnetic field with plasma $β=5$. We find that the magnetorotational instability (MRI) generates large-scale poloidal fields through non-axisymmetric shearing waves, with an additional contribution from axisymmetric induction through stretching by channel-like modes. The resulting mean fields become progressively weaker as the disk becomes thinner. Because these fields regulate MRI turbulence, thinner disks exhibit weaker angular-momentum transport and accrete more slowly than the standard $v_{\rm acc}\propto(h/r)^2$ thin-disk scaling would predict. The magnetic-flux transport velocity remains comparable to the accretion velocity, so weaker field generation and slower transport combine to strongly suppress black-hole flux accumulation at smaller $h/r$. Correspondingly, the thinnest disk ($h/r=0.1$) produces an electromagnetic jet efficiency of only $η_{\rm{EM}}\sim1\%$, while the thickest disk reaches the magnetically arrested disk (MAD) state and attains $η_{\rm{EM}}\geq100\%$. Using the measured large-scale magnetic flux distribution and transport velocities, we estimate the time required to accumulate MAD-level magnetic flux. Only the $h/r\sim0.3$ disk reaches MAD in the duration of our simulations, at $t\simeq2\times10^4\,r_g/c$, whereas for $h/r=0.1$ we estimate a timescale of $\sim10^8\,r_g/c$. These results link disk geometry to magnetic-flux accumulation and jet launching, with direct implications for the timescales over which jets can emerge in transient accreting systems.

title: Extreme eccentricity in double neutron stars without exotic physics
comment: Nature Astronomy, accepted August 14, 2026 (submitted April 11, 2026). This author's version differs slightly from the accepted manuscript. 55 pages, 16 figures, 3 tables (including Supplementary Information)
summary: The formation of neutron stars (NSs) underpins astrophysical phenomena from supernovae (SNe), radio pulsars and X-ray binaries to double NS mergers that power gravitational waves (GWs), short gamma-ray bursts and r-process kilonovae. A recently reported double NS (PSR J0653+0443) with record eccentricity e=0.9924 provides a unique laboratory for studying GW emission and orbital evolution, and challenges existing formation scenarios. Here we show that such extreme eccentricities arise naturally -- without invoking exotic conditions -- from standard binary-SN physics: instantaneous mass loss (Blaauw recoil) and natal kicks readily produce e>0.99 for both compact and wide pre-SN orbits. The observed orbit matches three families of kinematic solutions spanning a range of kick velocities and progenitor configurations. Physically motivated priors based on NS spin and pre-SN mass transfer constrain the viable progenitor family, demonstrating that the system is not exceptionally rare. Future proper-motion measurements will tightly constrain its natal SN kick magnitude.

title: The MARTINI platform II. Tracing r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers with long-lived remnants
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures
summary: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers are among the primary sites of the rapid neutron-capture (r-)process. In mergers with long-lived remnants, sustained neutrino irradiation raises the electron fraction of the disc wind ejecta, modifying the resulting nucleosynthesis pattern. Yields from numerical-relativity simulations with accurate neutrino transport are needed to quantify the contribution of BNS mergers to the Galactic production of heavy elements and to interpret kilonova spectra. We present and publicly release tracer trajectories and nucleosynthesis yields for eight BNS mergers forming long-lived neutron star remnants, obtained from general-relativistic simulations with M1 neutrino transport, spanning two equations of state (DD2 and SFHo), and a range of total masses and mass ratios. Passive tracer particles following the dynamical and wind ejecta were post-processed with the nuclear reaction network WinNet up to 1 Gyr. The yields and tracer trajectories are available on the MARTINI platform. At 1 day, the production of light and first-peak elements (He, Ni, Sr, and Y) is similar across models and is primarily enhanced by the neutrino-irradiated disc wind. The yields of heavy nuclei vary by more than one order of magnitude, with unequal-mass binaries producing the largest amounts owing to their more neutron-rich ejecta. Our He yields, particularly in the wind, exceed those of recent studies based on an M0 neutrino scheme, consistent with the stronger neutrino irradiation resulting from an M1 scheme. At 1 Gyr, all models reproduce the second and third solar r-process peaks, but differ in the first peak, the lanthanide region, the mass range between the first and second peaks, and the trans-lead region, reflecting the electron fraction distribution of the ejecta and the dynamical and wind contributions. Two equal-mass models provide a close match to the solar pattern.

title: Identifying Scientifically Interesting Galaxies with Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to the Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop (ML4PS 2026)
summary: Anomaly searches in large astronomical image datasets aim to identify rare objects for follow-up investigation. Yet the objects that are most statistically unusual are not necessarily those of greatest scientific relevance. We investigate whether pretrained vision-language models can directly assess scientific interest from natural-language instructions, enabling galaxy images to be ranked without labeled examples. We evaluate models on a 20,000-image Hubble Space Telescope sample that includes 167 reference anomalies previously identified through machine learning and expert inspection. By scoring images for scientific interest, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite places 98.2% of the reference anomalies within the highest-ranked ~2,000 images, at a present-day inference cost of approximately $5.05 per 10,000 images. We recover known gravitational lenses, jellyfish-galaxy candidates, and galaxies with visible jets, and release 102 high-scoring candidates for further investigation. These results show that an off-the-shelf vision-language model, without any training on the target data, offers a practical way to rank large image datasets by scientific relevance rather than rarity. The project code is available at https://github.com/TheCheng2005/Galaxy-Anomaly-Search/

title: Considering Numerical Relativity Surrogate Models for AGN Channel Merger Dynamics
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables
summary: Binary black hole mergers (BBH) are currently observed by the gravitational-wave detectors LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA (LVK). A fraction of these mergers are likely to originate in active galactic nuclei (AGN), but the details of the dynamical processes driving AGN channel mergers remain poorly understood. Monte Carlo For AGN Channel Testing and Simulation (McFACTS) is an open-source, public software used to simulate AGN channel BBH formation and evolution with configurable options for exploring various AGN and Nuclear Star Cluster (NSC) parameter options. Within McFACTS, BBH mergers evolve through gas drag and dynamical interactions, ignoring relativistic effects which can influence merger remnant properties. Here we demonstrate in McFACTS the effect of handing off inspiralling BBH to a numerical relativity (NR) surrogate model, which more accurately predicts the masses, spins, and kick velocities of merger remnants. Compared to a simple analytic approach to calculating merger and remnant properties the NR surrogate model is significantly more accurate at predicting remnant spins, which improve $χ_{eff}$ and $χ_{p}$ calculations, and recoil kicks, parameters especially important for higher generation BBH mergers. Our findings show the NR surrogate significantly changes distributions of remnant spins and kick velocities, as well as showing that alternative methods should be used cautiously in future studies. We also outline some simple models which are computationally efficient and can reproduce much of the NR surrogate model results.

title: NORI: a GPU-accelerated code for simulating self-gravitating and self-interacting dark matter
comment: 23 pages, 17 figures
summary: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can form cores in dark matter haloes and later drive their gravothermal collapse, raising their central densities far above those of NFW haloes. Simulating this collapse is computationally demanding, requiring increasingly short time-steps and a large particle number to resolve the shrinking core. We present NORI, an $N$-body code that runs on CPUs and GPUs and simulates isolated self-gravitating systems with elastic, isotropic self-interactions using a Monte-Carlo method. To avoid MPI communication in the tree walks, each compute node in CPU mode, and each GPU or group of GPUs in GPU mode, holds a copy of all particles and its own Morton-ordered tree. A fixed evaluation order makes the results bitwise identical on CPUs and GPUs. Applying scattering events sequentially conserves the momentum and energy of each pair to round-off and allows multiple scatterings per particle per step. With global time-steps in both codes, NORI is several times faster on CPUs than our AREPO-2 implementation. One four-A100 GPU node is up to 60 times faster per time-step than AREPO-2 on a 112-core CPU node. For a full core-collapse simulation, where AREPO-2 uses individual time-steps, the speed-up is $\sim 30$ for the central density to reach $10^3$--$10^4$ times the NFW scale density, $ρ_{\rm s}$. We follow a halo with $10^8$ particles within $r_{200}$ to a central density of $10^4\,ρ_{\rm s}$. Within the limit of about $2\times10^9$ particles set by data replication, NORI provides an efficient tool for isolated SIDM simulations, including gravothermal collapse and cluster collisions.

title: Validating an X-ray-based method for identifying Fermi blazars
summary:
Context. Blazars are the main population of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected in gamma rays by Fermi. However, around 34% of Fermi sources remain unidentified, partly due to their large positional uncertainties, motivating multiwavelength methods to identify possible counterparts.
  Aims. We evaluate a method proposed to identify BL Lacertae (BL Lac) candidates among unidentified Fermi sources based on their X-ray properties, using Swift-XRT observations.
  Methods. We examined published optical spectra for an initial sample of 148 X-ray-selected candidates. We found 71 sources with spectra spatially consistent with the proposed associations and reassessed their classifications using standard blazar criteria. We then compared these classifications with the method's initial predictions.
  Results. Of the 71 proposed counterparts, 80.28% are classified as BL Lac objects and 87.32% as possible gamma-ray-emitting AGNs, supporting the effectiveness of the X-ray-based selection. We also identify four Seyfert galaxies, suggesting that the method is sensitive to this class despite its rarity among gamma-ray emitters.
  Conclusions. Our results show that X-ray observations are effective for selecting BL Lac candidates among unidentified Fermi sources and support future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns. The high fraction of BL Lacs and AGNs suggests that blazars may account for a substantial part of the unidentified gamma-ray population. The Seyfert identifications also raise questions about the origin of high-energy emission in AGNs not typically associated with relativistic jets, highlighting the need for further multiwavelength observations.

title: Focal plane modal estimation of high-order wavefront drifts on coronagraphic testbeds
summary: The upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) requires precise wavefront stability over long observation periods to directly image Exo-Earths, which are 10 orders of magnitude dimmer than their host star. Dark zone maintenance (DZM) has been proposed as a focal plane high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC) strategy to mitigate thermal and mechanical instabilities that cause slow-evolving high-order wavefront drifts, which ultimately degrade contrast. Here we present a modal dark zone maintenance (MDZM) algorithm that uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the drifting wavefront modes in the basis of the deformable mirror (DM) actuators used for control. The estimator derives information across the entire focal plane from probe-pair images, addressing deficiencies of DZM, and directly obtains a DM command, eliminating the need for Electric Field Conjugation (EFC) and its regularization parameter. MDZM has been demonstrated in simulation and in hardware on the Decadal Survey Testbed (DST) at NASA JPL. These experiments have maintained a normalized intensity (NI) of $\sim 3 \times 10^{-10}$ for over 36 hours, and have reduced the gap to the photon-derived theoretical bounds compared to DZM. MDZM also provides an estimate of naturally occurring drift on the testbed, offering potential system identification capabilities. To evaluate the robustness of MDZM, a parameter scan is conducted on DST, spanning exposure times and drift rates. Additionally, realistic observing scenarios for HWO will involve broadband images with a 20% bandwidth, rather than the 2.5% narrowband images previously used in MDZM testbed demonstrations. Therefore, we tested MDZM in simulation using broadband sensing images with a 10% bandwidth, using the FALCO software package with a model based on DST, and compared its performance against MDZM runs using narrowband images.

title: Search for Eccentric Neutron Star-Black Hole Binaries in Advanced LIGO's Fourth Observing Run using Effective-One-Body Waveforms
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures, 1 table
summary: The observation of orbital eccentricity in compact binary coalescences would provide a direct signature of dynamical formation environments. Previous matched-filter searches for eccentric neutron star-black hole (NSBH) binaries have been severely limited by computational constraints, necessitating the use of simplified waveform models that capture secular dephasing but omit apsidal precession and inter-orbit harmonics. Including these physical features increases the sensitive search volume for systems with $0.2 \le e_{20} \le 0.28$ by $\sim 25\%$ to $30\%$. We present a rapid matched-filter search methodology that makes the direct use of time-domain effective-one-body waveforms computationally feasible. By multibanding and high-frequency ratio-filtering, our pipeline achieves a $\sim 20\times$ reduction in computational cost. This allows a bank of 88.6 million effective-one-body templates, fifteen times larger than prior eccentric analyses, to search O4a and O4b Advanced LIGO data. We recover the known low-mass mergers GW230518_125908 and GW230529_181500 with parameters consistent with zero eccentricity. Finding no new gravitational-wave events with orbital eccentricity ($e_{20} \ge 0.05$), we place $90\%$ credible upper limits on the local merger rate density of eccentric NSBH systems across the search space of $\mathcal{R}_{90\%} \le 7.5\text{-}57\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, up to a factor of $\sim 4$ improvement over previous observational bounds. At the parameters of GW200105_162426, this non-detection establishes an upper limit of $\mathcal{R}_{90\%} \le 12.1\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Alternatively, if GW200105_162426 is treated as an eccentric detection, the lack of subsequent detections in O4 updates the inferred local merger rate density of this population to $\mathcal{R} = 6.6^{+6.3}_{-3.8}\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.

title: Experimental Demonstration of Double-Fourier Interferometer Imaging for Future Space-Based Far-Infrared Observatories
summary: Far-infrared (FIR) astronomy is crucial for observing star formation, active galactic nuclei, and protoplanetary systems, but its effectiveness is severely limited by poor diffraction-limited spatial resolution. To overcome this limitation, a double-Fourier interferometer (DFI), which couples a spatial interferometer with a Fourier transform spectrometer, has been proposed to deliver high-resolution broadband spectral imaging. Despite various conceptual and prototype studies, a comprehensive demonstration of DFI capabilities has been lacking. In this study, we present the validation of key DFI observing techniques using a laboratory testbed operating in the 0.3 to 2.1 THz optical bandwidth. We detail the instrument's ideal response alongside necessary calibrations for intensity imbalances, non-linear phase errors, and phase-center offsets. Our experimental results successfully demonstrate aperture synthesis for both one- and two-dimensional targets, accurately recovering source geometries. Furthermore, we prove the instrument's sensitivity to spatially dependent spectral variations by utilizing a low-pass optical filter on extended sources. Finally, we validate wide-field imaging capabilities by combining data from independent pixels in a detector array, each sensitive to different regions of the source plane. The experimental data show significant agreement with theoretical predictions, with minor deviations attributed to optical aberrations and perspective effects. These laboratory demonstrations validate the DFI architecture as a highly capable and mature technology for future space-based FIR observatories.

title: Phase-resolved X-ray spectroscopy of the Vela pulsar with NICER observations
comment: 10 pages, 9 Figures, 5 Tables
summary: PSR J0835-4510 (a.k.a. the Vela pulsar) is the best studied pulsar in the Southern hemisphere given its high radio brightness and large glitch activity. However, its X-ray brightness is comparatively lower, making the study of its X-ray profile difficult. We aim to investigate the X-ray emission of the Vela pulsar coming from the surface of the neutron star to infer the properties of its hotspots and assess whether they share a common spectral shape. We also aim to prove whether the 2021 glitch affected the hotspots. We used ephemeris obtained from high-cadence radio observations with the radio telescopes of the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy to combine all the NICER observations of the Vela pulsar after its 2019 glitch and before its 2024 glitch. We obtained a folded pulse profile for three different energy ranges and subsequently studied their phase-resolved energy spectra. We additionally analyzed a Chandra observation to quantify the pulsar's contribution to the total soft X-ray emission detected by NICER, which cannot spatially resolve the pulsar from the surrounding pulsar wind nebula (PWN). The pulsar contribution to the total observed emission represents less than 40-45% of the flux below 0.9 keV, dropping to 3-4% in the 0.9-2.0 keV range and further down to ~2% above 2 keV, where the PWN fully dominates. We find that the X-ray folded profile of the Vela pulsar was not measurably perturbed by the 2021 glitch. We studied separately seven regions of the pulse profile. We found that all of them are well modeled by one or two blackbodies. The temperatures of these hotspots are between $0.79(7) \times 10^{6}$ K $\leq T \leq 4.8^{+0.8}_{-0.6} \times 10^{6}$ K, while their sizes vary between $0.048^{+0.016}_{-0.009}$ km $\leq R \leq 3.9^{+0.9}_{-0.6}$ km, and their luminosities between $5\times10^{30}$ erg/s $\lesssim L < 1\times10^{32}$ erg/s.

title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry
summary: Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.

title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
comment: 18 pages of main text with 10 figures; 2 appendices. Constructive community feedback welcomed in advance of submission
summary: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.

title: Characterisation of the ILMT 4K x 4K TDI CCD imager
summary: In this work, we determine the gain and read-out noise of the 4Kx4K CCD imager used with the 4-m International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT). Due to the zenith-pointing characteristic of the telescope, the CCD operates in the Time Delay Integration (TDI) mode for image acquisition. The CCD frames obtained during rising twilight have non-uniform illumination and can potentially be used to calculate important CCD parameters using two approaches. The first approach directly measures variance in flux along rows with minimum horizontal gradient, despite the strong vertical illumination gradient. The second method divides the CCD frame into regions exposed to similar background illumination and analyses the flux ratio variation between the two regions. Mathematically, we establish a linear relationship between the signal variance and average flux, from which gain is determined, while the read-out noise (RON) is measured independently from the bias frames. Both methods provide a gain value of approximately 3.9 e/ADU, while the RON measured from bias frames is 1.55 ADU (~ 6 e). Estimation of these parameters provides a better understanding of the CCD performance and allows for an accurate calibration.

title: A Spectral-model-independent Diagnostic of Phase-resolved Spectral Convergence in Swift J0243.6+6124
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures (4 main-text figures and 3 appendix figures)
summary: We introduce a spectral-model-independent spectral-shape metric, $δ_{\rm rms}$, to probe phase-resolved spectral evolution in the Galactic ultraluminous X-ray pulsar Swift J0243.6+6124. The $δ_{\rm rms}$--luminosity relation reveals a reproducible convergence--redivergence behavior: spectra from two geometrically opposite pulse phases converge to near identity around $L_{\rm t}^{\ast}\sim8.8\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$, with a mean shape difference of only $\sim2\%$, and rediverge at higher luminosities, most prominently at higher energies. This strong phase-resolved spectral convergence coincides with a pulse-profile reversal and traces the same transition luminosities previously identified from broadband continuum evolution, including $L_{\rm t}\sim4.5\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$. These results suggest a possible luminosity-driven reweighting between a broadly distributed surface-reprocessed/reflected component and an increasingly important direct accretion-column contribution, while establishing $δ_{\rm rms}$ as a robust, spectral-model-independent diagnostic of radiation-geometry restructuring in bright accreting X-ray pulsars.

title: PyMsOfa 2.0: A Pure-Python Implementation of the IAU Standards of Fundamental Astronomy Service
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures
summary: Astrometric calculations require authoritative algorithms so that every result is correct and reproducible. The Standards of Fundamental Astronomy (SOFA) service of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) provides such algorithms, officially released only in Fortran 77 and ANSI C. In an earlier paper we presented the first version of PyMsOfa, a Python package wrapping the SOFA C library. Here we present PyMsOfa 2.0, which re-implements the complete SOFA library in pure Python with NumPy. All 247 official SOFA routines are ported directly to Python, requiring no compilation of any external C library and running identically on Linux, Windows, and macOS. The routines operate on NumPy arrays, so arguments can be processed in batch, which is convenient for survey pipelines and Monte Carlo simulations. The package also provides an extension module with validated models not yet part of the official SOFA release, such as the improved precession--nutation model IAU 2006$_{J_2}$/2000A$_{R26}$. The reimplementation reproduces the official SOFA algorithms: all constants, series, and coefficients are taken unchanged from the SOFA source files, and routine names differ only by the pym prefix. We verify every routine against the official SOFA C release: most reproduce the C results to machine precision, the remainder within the accuracy tolerance stated in the SOFA documentation. The package has been applied to Gaia astrometric reduction and used in astrometric studies of the Closeby Habitable Exoplanet Survey (CHES) mission, and is available through PyPI, GitHub, and Zenodo.

title: Numerical Simulations of the interaction between winds from tidal disruption event and supermassive black hole circumnuclear medium
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, accepted by APJ
summary: The interaction between winds from tidal disruption event (TDE) and the circumnuclear medium (CNM) around supermassive black holes is believed to contribute to the radio emission of non-jetted TDEs. This model has been studied both analytically and numerically. In previous works, the properties of wind are usually set to be angle-independent. It is not clear to what extent the results deviate from those in the case where TDE wind properties are angle-dependent. We perform numerical simulations to investigate the effects of the angular distribution of wind properties on the radio light curve in the wind-CNM interaction model. We find that given that the wind mass and kinetic energy fixed, the radio light curve in the optically thin waveband significantly depends on the angle-dependence of wind properties. Even when the swept-up CNM mass is still less than the wind mass, a slight deceleration can affect the light curve. Changing the angular dependence of the wind properties causes the deceleration to vary across angles. Consequently, the final light curve--the time evolution of radiation integrated over all angles--would differ significantly from that predicted in models with a spatially uniform wind injection. This can result in a slower rise or a faster decline (depending on the CNM profile) than the analytical prediction, and can even turn the rise phase into a long-lasting plateau. Therefore, it is essential to carefully take into account the angular dependence of wind properties to study the wind-CNM interaction.

title: Shock detection in meshless finite mass hydrodynamic schemes
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures, comments welcome
summary: Shocks are prevalent in a multitude of astrophysical plasmas. They are essential in the dissipation of gravitational potential energy during structure formation, where they channel it into heat, turbulence, magnetic fields, and particle acceleration. Accurately capturing shocks in simulations of cosmological structure formation is a considerable challenge, due to the complexity of overlapping and colliding shocks, embedded in a medium experiencing complex shear flows. Fully Lagrangian hydrodynamical methods have historically been inferior in this regard compared to Eulerian or pseudo-Lagrangian methods. This work aims to remedy this discrepancy. We present the first efforts to implement a shockfinder algorithm with shock surface reconstruction for meshless finite mass (MFM) hydrodynamic schemes. We show its accuracy compared to analytic predictions and a legacy smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)- based shock-finding method. We apply this new shock-finding method to simulations of cosmic structure formation to obtain improved predictions for shock energy dissipation and cosmic ray (CR) acceleration.

title: Migration Traps as Variability Attractors. II. Nonmonotonic X-Ray Timing Signatures of Embedded Stellar-Mass Black Holes in AGN Disks
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Stellar-mass black holes (sBHs) embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks may affect X-ray variability through magnetic reconnection. As sBHs migrate and accumulate near migration traps, they disturb the disk magnetic field and trigger reconnection events that heat the disk and eject plasma into the overlying corona. The injected plasma dissipates kinetic energy and can trigger the release of magnetic energy already stored in the corona. We calculate the resulting coronal X-ray emission and the disk ultraviolet (UV) variability, including the disk thermal response and reprocessing of incident X-rays. We find that embedded sBHs can initially enhance short-timescale X-ray variability, but the variability becomes suppressed as more sBHs accumulate in the disk. At higher mass accretion rates through AGN disks, this suppression appears earlier. As sBH-associated reconnection events become more frequent, their active regions increasingly overlap, reducing the magnetic energy available to each event from the corona. We also find that variations in the disk ultraviolet (UV) emission follow the X-ray variations with a shorter delay than in the model without sBHs. These results suggest that a growing population of embedded sBHs does not necessarily produce stronger short-timescale X-ray variability.

title: lenscape: Fast, High-resolution $Δχ^2$ Maps of Microlensing Events
comment: Accepted for publication in AAS journals; 1 figure; code available at https://github.com/hippke/lenscape
summary: Planetary microlensing analyses rely on $Δχ^2$ maps across the binary-lens separation $s$ and mass ratio $q$ to locate degenerate solutions and bound parameter uncertainties. Because every grid point requires a full light-curve optimization with finite-source magnifications, constructing these maps is often the primary computational bottleneck in event modeling. Here I present lenscape, an open-source Python package that accelerates $Δχ^2$ mapping and suppresses local-minimum artifacts through multi-stage neighbor propagation and adaptive contour refinement. Applied to the planetary event MOA-2022-BLG-091, lenscape reproduces the published $50\times50$ map in 14 minutes and generates a $400\times400$ map in under two hours on a desktop computer.

title: Black Hole Spin Evolution in Magnetized Accretion Flows
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures (3 in appendix). Comments welcome. Submitted for publication
summary: Black hole (BH) spin grows as accretion supplies angular momentum and decreases as magnetically driven jets remove it, driving the BH toward an equilibrium spin, $a_{\rm \star; eq}$. Existing estimates of $a_{\rm \star; eq}$ rely on general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations with fixed BH mass and spin, and cover only the extreme limits of horizon magnetic flux $φ\rightarrow0$ and magnetically arrested disks (MADs), $φ\approxφ_{\rm MAD}$. We evolve the BH mass and spin in long 3D GRMHD simulations of radiatively inefficient accretion flows aligned or anti-aligned with the BH spin. We find the spin-up parameter as a function of BH spin and $φ/φ_{\rm MAD}$, and derive the equilibrium spin as a continuous function of flux, $a_{\rm \star; eq}(φ/φ_{\rm MAD})$. The equilibrium spin falls steeply with flux, from $a_{\rm \star; eq}\approx0.9$ in weakly magnetized flows through $a_{\rm \star; eq}(φ/φ_{\rm MAD}=0.5)\approx0.5$ to $a_{\rm \star; eq}(φ/φ_{\rm MAD}=1)\approx0.06$ in sustained MADs. In weakly magnetized flows, a slowly spinning BH must accrete at least its initial mass to reach equilibrium, whereas MADs spin down rapidly rotating BHs after accreting less than half of it. However, as the BH grows, the growing gravitational radius and enhanced inflow reduce $φ/φ_{\rm MAD}$, driving disks whose magnetic-flux supply cannot keep pace out of the MAD state and allowing the BH to transition from spin-down to spin-up. The final spin thus depends on both the magnetic flux history and the accreted mass. We discuss implications for a variety of BH-powered engines and provide a subgrid prescription for galaxy-scale simulations and population studies.

title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
comment: 22 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

title: Simultaneous Real-Color Time-Domain Survey of the Coma Field with the Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto)
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures and 3 tables. Comments welcome!
summary: We present the results from a high-cadence, multi-channel time-domain survey targeting the Coma galaxy cluster, utilizing the newly commissioned 1.6-m Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto). Mephisto's pioneering mosaic focal-plane design enables strictly simultaneous imaging in three distinct optical bands ($u/v, g/r, i/z$). This unique capability allows for the extraction of true, instantaneous spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of fast-evolving transients. Our survey continuously monitors a 20-square-degree footprint centered on the Coma cluster. By strategically targeting this massive local structure, we exploit cosmic anisotropy to significantly amplify the volumetric discovery rate of stellar explosions. During the initial six-month pilot operation, we successfully detected and tracked nine new supernovae (SNe). Remarkably, our high-cadence, multi-band strategy allowed us to capture ultra-early rising light curves and pre-discovery signals (e.g., SN 2026dyr) hours to days prior to formal discovery alerts. These instantaneous early-phase colors allow us to reconstruct intrinsic SEDs without temporal interpolation, providing reliable constraints on the physical parameters of early supernova (SN) evolution. Furthermore, our observed supernova yield shows good agreement with theoretical forecasts based on local stellar mass and star-formation rate overdensities. These pilot results validate the efficiency of the Mephisto Coma survey, demonstrating its objective capability to systematically explore the local transient population and provide rapid optical localizations for future multi-messenger events.

title: SuperCrude EoS: A Simple, Analytical, and Reasonably Accurate Equation of State for Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
comment: ApJ Submitted
summary: We present SuperCrude, a vastly simplified astrophysical equation of state that captures the most important physics needed for explosive astrophysics, but using compact, physically-motivated analytical approximations rather than precise interpolated data tables. We present a number of code tests demonstrating the performance of SuperCrude in a wide range of parameter space. In large regions of parameter space, SuperCrude is precisely accurate to within the accuracy level of helmeos. For some regions (especially where degeneracy, gas, and radiation are comparable) SuperCrude has errors in its effective adiabatic index on the order of a few percent. The solver's estimate of the temperature is less accurate, on the order of tens of percent. Because the solver is analytic, SuperCrude is designed in such a way to guarantee exact thermodynamic consistency. We incorporate SuperCrude into some hydrodynamic and astrophysical test problems, including the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf star. When coupled with a stiff nuclear network, SuperCrude does not achieve the same nucleosynthetic yields as helmeos, motivating future work to improve the temperature accuracy further.

title: Harmonic brightness oscillations point to magnetar giant flares in rare short gamma-ray bursts
comment: 57 pages, 9 figures; Authors' version of the article published in Science Advances, available at https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/sciadv.aee6388
summary: Kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) have been observed in a few rare gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), but their physical origin remains uncertain. We reanalyze the two short GRBs with reported kilohertz QPOs, GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A, and find evidence for possible harmonic-like organization around a characteristic frequency scale near 360 hertz. The similar harmonic-like pattern in GRB 910711 and in the confirmed magnetar giant flare (MGF) event GRB 200415A, including features extending above 4 kilohertz, points to timing phenomenology on frequency scales relevant to magnetar oscillation modes. The temporal and spectral similarities between the two events and the difficulty of explaining these features in merger-driven scenarios favor an MGF-like interpretation of GRB 910711. This timing phenomenology may therefore provide an additional observational handle, complementary to spectral, temporal, and localization information, for distinguishing rare MGF-like transients from merger-driven GRBs.

title: Flow-based neural networks for scalable high resolution imaging of VLBI observations
comment: Published in MNRAS
summary: Bayesian sampling methods in very-long-baseline interferometry enable reliable imaging of astronomical sources with a record high angular resolution. However, even after the transition from classical MCMC methods to flow-based neural networks, they remain computationally expensive as the number of recovered features grows. We used WaveletFlow neural network architecture to increase the number of pixels in the recovered image distribution, addressing the scaling issues of previous models. We applied the algorithm to both model data and archive RadioAstron project observations of M87 and ALMA telescope observations of HL Tau. While yielding comparable fidelity of the individual images, the algorithm provides more statistical information compared to CLEAN, which may be crucial for future research on compact astronomical objects such as active galactic nuclei.

title: XRISM/Resolve Study of Large Scale Properties in Tycho's Supernova Remnant
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: Resolve, the microcalorimeter array aboard the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM), provides an unprecedented spectral view of Tycho's Supernova Remnant (SNR). We fit the X-ray spectra of the five public archival XRISM observations of the SNR with a multi-component non-equilibrium ionization plasma model assuming spherical expansion and a uniform abundance pattern. For pointings away from the center of the object, we divide each into three spectra based on angular distance from the remnant's geometric center and fit all three simultaneously with the center-pointing observation. We tie elemental abundances together across all model components. We find that pseudo-spherical expansion fits well the Tycho SNR in the regions where Resolve has observed, although iron appears slower on the approaching side than the receding side. We also find that a close-to-uniform abundance pattern across the SNR is consistent with these data.

title: The Korean Space Telescope (KST): A Dedicated Space Observatory for the Dark Universe
comment: 55 pages, 21 figures, 11 tables. White paper for the Korean Space Telescope (KST). To be Submitted to the Journal of the Korean Astronomical Society (JKAS)
summary: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.

title: A universal relation predicts the observed reversal of a supernova chirp
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: Superluminous supernovae, among the brightest stellar explosions, are thought to be powered by newborn magnetars. One such event, SN 2024afav, ``chirped'', displaying sinusoidal, increasing-frequency ($P(99\textrm{ d})\sim39\pm8$ d to $P(166\textrm{ d})\sim17\pm5$ d) light-curve modulations. The model explaining this chirp, a precessing disk falling onto the dimming magnetar, generalizes to a normalization-independent universal relation between the period derivative and the dimming rate of the light curve. Applied to the published chirp alone, with the spin-down time measured from the unmodulated light curve, the relation predicts that the chirp must halt near $t \approx 150$ d and reverse. With continued follow-up of SN 2024afav, we report the discovery of five new modulations in which the chirp reverses ($P(177\textrm{ d})\sim24\pm4$ d to $P(208\textrm{ d})\sim38\pm2$ d) at $t=147\pm3$ d, as predicted. Applied to chirping events from upcoming surveys, the relation could identify the precession mechanism and disk physics of each engine.

title: Tabular Foundation Models Dramatically Outperform Bespoke Photometric Redshift Estimators
comment: Accepted for 9th Workshop on Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences (ML4PS 2026)
summary: Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning. Evaluating on a widely used benchmark dataset, we find that TFMs predicting full probability distributions in a single forward pass systematically outperform bespoke estimators across both representative and biased training data regimes, matching or exceeding baselines trained on over $40{,}000$ galaxies with just $1{,}000$ training context examples. We also show that the TFM advantage is largest when little to no calibration data are available, and that it persists even when the bespoke baselines are supplemented with up to $10{,}000$ representative calibration spectra. This shows that TFMs offer a sample-efficient framework for upcoming imaging-only astronomical surveys, where observational selection bias can be mitigated simply by including a small representative calibration sample in context.

title: The Disk Awakens: IXPE's Sequel Observation of GS 1354-64 Suggests Changing-Look Behavior in the Steep-Power-Law State
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to ApJ
summary: After decades of only failed transitions, the black hole X-ray binary GS 1354-64 has undergone a complete outburst again. We present its first X-ray polarimetric investigation in the fading steep-power-law (SPL) state, following an earlier intermediate-state IXPE campaign during the same outburst. The 2-8 keV emission has a polarization degree (PD) of 2.3 +/- 0.2% and polarization angle (PA) of 5 +/- 3 degrees. Compared with the intermediate state, where PD=3.9 +0.3/-0.2% and PA=-2 +/-2 degrees, the broadband PD is lower while the PA remains consistent. The intermediate-state type-C quasi-periodic oscillation state has also disappeared, marking a major reconfiguration of the accretion flow. Assuming a distance of 7 kpc, the observed the intensity drop from 2.5% to 1.6% of the Eddington luminosity over 10.2 days is punctuated by several broad hour-to-day-scale troughs, tracing two distinct tracks in hardness-intensity space. Simultaneous spectroscopy shows the troughs' spectra contains a cooler disk with smaller apparent normalization, while no change in the Compton component's photon index or normalization is required between tracks. The model-independent analysis identifies a steeper increase in PD with energy outside the troughs, yielding G_E=1.5 +/- 0.2%/keV, compared with G_E=0.7 +0.3/-0.5%/keV during the troughs. Their duration and spectropolarimetric morphology distinguish the troughs from traditional short absorption dips seen in X-ray binaries, providing a possible stellar-mass analog of the recurrent accretion changes that drive "changing-look" behavior in supermassive black hole systems.

title: Towards an Astronomical Use of New-Generation Geodetic Observations
comment: PhD thesis, Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM). Supervisors: Iván Martí-Vidal and Rafael Bachiller García. Defended on 19 October 2026. 230 pages
summary:
This thesis explores the astronomical use of observations from the VLBI Global Observing System (VGOS), a next-generation geodetic network designed to improve the precision of terrestrial and celestial reference frames and Earth orientation parameters. Although primarily conceived for geodesy, its wide frequency coverage and regular monitoring of compact active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable opportunities for astrophysics.
  We develop a calibration pipeline that transforms VGOS correlator outputs into full-polarization, calibrated visibilities suitable for astronomical imaging. The procedure combines linear-to-circular polarization conversion, instrumental phase and amplitude calibration, and a new wideband global fringe-fitting algorithm that accounts for dispersive ionospheric effects. Regularized maximum likelihood imaging is then used to reconstruct multi-frequency intensity and polarimetric images.
  The pipeline is applied to the blazar 1803+784 and five additional AGN: 3C418, 0059+581, 0613+570, 1849+670, and 2229+695. We measure frequency-dependent core shifts, spectral indices, and Faraday rotation properties. For 1803+784, the fitted core-shift index is $k_r = 0.73^{+0.12}_{-0.19}$, suggesting departures from a simple conical jet in energy equipartition.
  Finally, we apply the reconstructed source models to correct structure-dependent effects in geodetic VLBI observables. The correction reduces closure-delay scatter and post-fit residuals for strongly structured sources, particularly 3C418, while its effectiveness depends on source variability and the temporal proximity of the imaging observations.
  These results demonstrate the dual scientific value of VGOS as a powerful multi-frequency astronomical VLBI instrument and as a means of improving geodetic measurements.

title: RAKI: High-Order Alternative Finite Differences for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 1 table
summary: Binary neutron star (BNS) and black hole--neutron star mergers are among the most important multimessenger sources. Observations of these events could provide valuable insights into several unresolved phenomena, ranging from the efficiency of magnetic field amplification during and after mergers to the formation of magnetars and jets. Understanding these phenomena requires accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution, which remains a challenge for state-of-the-art general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In this work, we present \texttt{RAKI} (Relativistic Astrophysics Code Implementation of the Alternative Finite Difference Approach for GRMHD), the first GRMHD code to simulate BNS mergers using high-order alternative finite-difference methods with adaptive-order WENO (AFD-WENO-AO) reconstruction and a fully non-staggered, node-centred vector-potential formulation. The code achieves up to ninth-order convergence in smooth test problems while accurately capturing discontinuities. In magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) star tests, \texttt{RAKI} retains $99.2$ per cent of the initial maximum magnetic field strength over ${\sim}2$ ms, exhibiting an order of magnitude less magnetic field loss than a reference GRMHD code at the same resolution. In BNS merger simulations, fifth-order AFD-WENO-AO reconstruction yields approximately third-order convergence of the gravitational-wave phase in both magnetised and unmagnetised models. The discrete no-monopole constraint is preserved to machine precision without staggered grids, even during BNS mergers with moving refinement regions. These results establish \texttt{RAKI} as a high-order, non-staggered GRMHD framework for accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution in neutron star mergers and its implications for multimessenger astrophysics.

title: Search for Cosmic Rays in GRANDProto300
comment: Presented at the 60th Rencontres de Moriond on Very High Energy Phenomena in the Universe (Moriond VHEPU 2026). 4 pages, 1 figure
summary: GRANDProto300 is a prototype array of the GRAND experiment, designed to validate the technique of autonomous radio-detection of astroparticles by detecting cosmic rays with energies between 10$^{17} - 10^{18.5}$ eV. This observation will further enable the study of the Galactic-to-extragalactic source transition region. Between November 2024 and June 2025, 46 antennas were operational, and since July 2025, 63 antennas have been collecting data stably. We present here our cosmic-ray search pipeline, that involves several filtering steps: (1) exclusion of clustered (in time and space) noise events, (2) polarization cut, (3) zenith arrival cut, and (4) delay in expected trigger cut. The efficiency is evaluated on the latest batch of data from July 2025 to October 2025. Additionally, we present an identification layer that is being developed: a CNN-based algorithm to discriminate between noise and cosmic-ray signals, using signal traces. We present the accuracy of our model, trained both on simulations and on real cosmic-ray signal datasets.

title: The first mass peak of merging black holes from core binding energies and jet-driven explosions
comment: Will submit to PASP in two days to allow for comments; 11 pages, 5 figures
summary: We show that the jittering-jets explosion mechanism (JJEM) can qualitatively reproduce the shape of the black hole (BH) mass distribution observed by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA and quantitatively reproduce the peak around $M_{p1} \simeq 10 M_\odot$. To show this, we construct a toy model that captures the JJEM physics that explodes all massive stars, even when BHs form. According to the JJEM, BHs form when the star's binding energy is large, implying a massive progenitor with initial mass $M_i \gtrsim 25 M_\odot$, and when jets are launched along a fixed axis, implying a rapidly rotating pre-collapse stellar core. In this case, the jets are launched along the core's angular momentum and are inefficient at removing mass near the equatorial plane; when the stellar binding energy is large, a large fraction of the equatorial mass is accreted to form the BH. The toy model includes two parameters: the threshold binding energy in the core for BH formation and the jet opening angle along the poles. Although our finding is encouraging for the JJEM, future hydrodynamical simulations must determine the exact condition for BH formation in the JJEM and the BH mass.

authors: Nils Heyer for the RNO-G Collaboration
title: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) - System Design and Instrumentation
comment: Presented at the Topical Workshop on Electronics for Particle Physics - TWEPP2026
summary: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to measure cosmic neutrinos in the EeV range through an array of radio antennas detecting nanosecond-long radio flashes. In this contribution, the RNO-G electronic system is outlined, illustrating how signals are measured from the antennas to the recorded pulses. We present new instrumentation developments, focusing on electric melters to install LPDA antennas into the Greenlandic ice sheet. The new system will simplify deployment and reduce positioning uncertainty to $\pm$2cm (x/y) and $\pm$1°(rotational). We report on field tests from the RNO-G site at Summit Station.

title: Tidal disruption or plunge: the role of neutron star internal structure in black hole-neutron star mergers
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures
summary: The outcome of black hole--neutron star (BHNS) mergers is studied using a general-relativistic mass-shedding condition in the Kerr spacetime, which determines the tidal-disruption radius from the mass ratio, the black hole (BH) spin, the neutron star (NS) compactness, and the ratio of central to average density, $η=\frac{ρ_{c}}{\barρ}$. Comparing this radius with the innermost stable circular orbit, we map the boundary between tidal disruption and plunge for two relativistic mean-field equations of state (EOSs) and for an ensemble of about $10^4$ agnostic EOSs spanning the current uncertainty in the NS radius. We find that the disruption threshold is set mainly by the compactness, but NSs with the same compactness and different $η$ can have different outcomes. Using the tidal disruption radius, we construct a remnant-mass model calibrated against 70 numerical-relativity simulations, which reproduces the remnant mass with an accuracy comparable to existing fits. Applying the disruption criterion and the remnant model to GW200105, GW200115, and the candidate BHNS event GW230529, we find that GW200105 and GW200115 are consistent with a direct plunge. GW230529 lies close to the disruption threshold and may have undergone marginal disruption, leaving only a low-mass remnant.

title: Robust statistical significance for Gravitational Wave inference
comment: 9 pages including bibliography, 6 figures
summary: The field of gravitational-wave data analysis heavily relies on Bayes factors to make statements about astrophysical effects in events detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration. This is true on an event level, for example when discussing the potential detection of precession or eccentricity, as well as on a population level. For the latter, perhaps the main limiting factor is the reliance on the output from event-level nested sampling analyses, which is known to introduce growing uncertainties and biases as the number of detections increases. In both cases, while Bayes factors are useful when comparing different models, because the underlying distribution of Bayes factors in noise is unknown, it is often not possible to use them to make quantifiable statistical statements. Their statistical meaning is also questionable in the at least $20\%$ of gravitational-wave events that contain transient noise artifacts. This paper shows that it is possible to use evidence networks, which can infer Bayes factors after learning the distinguishability between datasets, to solve all of the aforementioned problems. By being able to calculate up to $10^5$ Bayes factors per second, we can construct background distributions of Bayes factors under different signal assumptions to estimate significance. We show that the high precision achieved allows us to scale the results from up to $10^4$ events with no discernable bias on population-level quantities, while laying the foundations for a likelihood-free method that does not rely on the assumption of Gaussian and stationary noise.

title: VERITAS Limits on Dark Matter Annihilation in the Galactic Center Halo
summary: Well-motivated models of particle dark matter predict its self-annihilation into Standard Model end states, which may be detected by particle detectors or telescopes. We conduct an indirect dark matter search using gamma rays detected by the VERITAS telescope from within $2^\circ$ of the Galactic Center. A template-based approach is used for background estimation, increasing our sensitivity to sources of gamma-ray emission with spatial extents comparable to the $3.5^\circ$ VERITAS field of view. The analysis benefits from data taken exclusively at large zenith angles, which results in an increased effective area at energies above ~1 TeV, compared to small zenith angle observations. No significant gamma-ray signal is observed in the search region, resulting in upper limits on the end-state-dependent dark matter annihilation cross sections. Cross sections as low as $\langle σ_\text{ann} v\rangle = 1.77\times 10^{-25} \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$ are excluded at 95% confidence assuming complete annihilation into $τ^+ τ^-$, an Einasto profile, and a dark matter mass of 1 TeV.

title: Preparation of a celestial field for precise VLBI observations of the JUICE spacecraft: a test case of the Venus flyby
comment: 13 pages, 6 tables, 6 figures. Accepted for publication in PASA
summary: The Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer mission, launched in 2023, is on its way to the Jovian system, to arrive in 2031. The Planetary Radio Interferometry and Doppler Experiment performs radio astronomical observations of the spacecraft already in its interplanetary cruise phase. Since the sky density of potential compact radio sources suitable as phase-reference calibrators in very long baseline interferometry observations is low, densifying the celestial reference frame along the Ecliptic is an essential task in support of JUICE. In preparation for the JUICE gravity assist manoeuvre at Venus in August 2025, to support the accurate reconstruction of the spacecraft state vector, we selected in-beam calibrator source candidates along the JUICE trajectory. Additionally, we attempted to link known nearby bright compact reference sources from the Radio Fundamental Catalog to the International Celestial Reference Frame. We performed nodding-style phase-referencing VLBI observations with the European VLBI Network at 8.4GHz, targeting nine in-beam calibrator candidate and three RFC sources in the celestial vicinity of JUICE's trajectory during its Venus flyby. We linked their positions to nearby ICRF sources by means of relative astrometry. Four of the ICC targets and all RFC sources were detected and imaged with the EVN, and their coordinates determined with typically sub-mas precision. Although none of the targeted ICC sources proved suitable as VLBI phase-reference calibrators because of being too faint or resolved, their newly-determined positions and flux densities could in principle be used to verify the detection of the spacecraft at the time of the actual flyby around Venus. During the detailed analysis of the ICC targets, we found that the structure of one of them, J0843+1826 is resolved on mas scale, and the other one, J0843+1814 is a young radio galaxy, likely a member of a cluster.

title: KM3-230213A: The Highest-Energy Cosmic Neutrino
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 1 table. Published in Physics and the Cosmos (2026)
summary: High-energy neutrinos provide a unique probe of the most extreme non-thermal processes in the Universe. The detection of the ultra-high-energy neutrino event KM3-230213A by the KM3NeT neutrino telescope, with an inferred parent-neutrino energy of O(10^17 eV), represents a major step forward in neutrino astronomy. In this review, we summarize the main properties of the event and discuss its interpretation within different astrophysical and cosmological scenarios, including active galactic nuclei, transient sources, and cosmogenic neutrinos, highlighting the role of multi-messenger constraints. Despite extensive follow-up observations, no unambiguous electromagnetic counterpart has been identified, and the event remains in tension with the absence of comparable detections in other experiments. This situation leaves open the possibility of more complex source scenarios or contributions from physics beyond the Standard Model. We also discuss the implications for the ultra-high-energy neutrino landscape and the prospects for future observations with next-generation detectors. KM3-230213A provides a unique opportunity to probe particle acceleration and neutrino production at energies far beyond the reach of terrestrial experiments.

title: Identifying narrow-band mutual coupling resonances in SKA-low stations using frequency-independent current basis functions
summary: Mutual coupling between closely spaced elements in aperture arrays introduces narrow-band spectral features in the Embedded Element Patterns (EEPs), threatening measurements of the 21-cm power spectrum with instruments such as SKA-low. We detail a method to identify such features through the construction of frequency-independent current basis functions, utilising a singular value decomposition of frequency-dependent basis functions. We demonstrate the method on a three-element linear array and full pseudo-random station of SKA log-periodic antennas and examine the current power induced by mutual coupling. For the pseudo-random layout station we note many narrow-band resonance features, including strong resonances at 50.8~MHz and 83.6~MHz, where the coupled power on the passive antennas can approach or exceed that of the excited antenna. Simulated delay power spectra for the SKA-low core show that observing in frequency bands including resonance features causes large foreground leakage within the delay power spectra, obscuring the EoR window. For the pseudo-random layout station with SKALA4.0 we identify two significant frequency bands from 59.2--76.2~MHz and 84.2--103.3~MHz which are free of contamination from current resonances, preserving the EoR window in these frequency ranges.

title: From photons to neutrinos : Advancing multi-messenger modeling with Gammapy
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, conference proceedings of Gamma 2026
summary: In recent years, several astrophysical objects have been identified as potential multi-messenger photon-neutrino emitters. New instruments dedicated to the study of these two messengers have been and are still being built, achieving unprecedented sensitivity. This observational improvement increases the need for more sophisticated and precise analysis tools. Multi-wavelength and multi-messenger data fitting is crucial to constrain astrophysical models of particle acceleration and radiation mechanisms at work in these extreme environments. In this contribution, we present a novel framework dedicated to multi-wavelength and multi-messenger modeling, built within the open-source software Gammapy. The framework enables data analysis from optical up to very-high-energy gamma rays, and fitting physical models directly to instrumental counts in these wavebands, without the need of computing flux points. Focusing on blazars as a first example of a multi-messenger candidate, we showcase the performance of this tool in constraining multi-wavelength emission models, and how it reduces fitting biases. We show the results of a leptonic model that can be fitted on the fly, due to the short computing time needed. For more computing-intensive emission codes, we explore a grid-fitting approach. We evaluate the performance of the new fitting tool and present its first application to leptonic modeling of blazars. By fitting directly on photon and neutrino events, this novel approach will enable, for the first time, statistically sound constraints on the physics of multi-messenger sources.

title: Temporal regularization of petal modes in SCAO systems: The Soft-Limiter approach
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 13 pages, 9 figures
summary: Extremely large telescopes (ELTs) rely on segmented mirrors and thick support structures that fragment the pupil. In single-conjugate AO (SCAO), this produces differential pistons, or petal modes. The Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (PWFS), baseline for ANDES, MICADO, HARMONI, and GMT-NGSAO, has poor sensitivity to these modes in the visible under realistic residual turbulence. We aim to prevent the "Island Effect", where poorly observed differential pistons accumulate and degrade the PSF, without compromising continuous-mode correction. We propose the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) Soft-Limiter, a deterministic, lightweight controller combining a subspace MMSE estimator derived from von Kármán priors with a continuous temporal regularization. It acts as a leaky integrator applied only to the relative petal degrees of freedom. End-to-end SPECULA simulations of ELT/ANDES show that, while a classical integrator loses lock and wanders across multiple fringes at seeing $\ge 1.0''$, the MMSE Soft-Limiter confines the differential piston within a single fringe over the $0.6-1.2''$ range. It bounds the petal excursion and its science-band impact under severe turbulence, while keeping optimal continuous-mode correction at good seeing, without the Strehl penalty of spatial mitigation such as Edge Actuator Coupling. We derive and verify the operating window for the leakage gain, $g \lesssim g_{\mathrm{eff}}/π$: below it, the fast loop retains genuine physical steps up to $λ_{WFS}/2$ with a small droop. This maintains a stable modulo-$λ_{WFS}$ wavefront on the fast sensor, letting a slower phasing sensor resolve integer ambiguities. As the window narrows with turbulence, its boundaries cross near $1.0''$ seeing; beyond this, retaining physical discontinuities becomes the sole responsibility of the phasing channel, a key design driver for segmented ELTs.

title: A Candidate Binary Microlensing Event in the 2018 Gamma-Ray Flare of 3C 279
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures
summary: The April 2018 gamma-ray flare of the flat-spectrum radio quasar 3C~279 exhibited sharp peaks within a broader outburst. Its rapid substructure was previously attributed to magnetic reconnection. Motivated by its distinctive temporal profile within our comparison sample of bright blazar flares and its resemblance to caustic-crossing features in optical microlensing events, we investigate a finite-source binary-microlensing interpretation. A jointly fitted model of binary-lens magnification, a smooth intrinsic flare, and Gaussian-process variability reproduces the principal double-peaked structure of the GeV light curve. The adopted local solution has a binary mass ratio of $q\simeq0.098$ and an Einstein timescale of $t_{\rm E}\simeq0.327$~d. The absolute lens mass and projected source radius depend on the lens distance and relative proper motion. The fitted geometry can correspond to a Galactic planetary-mass binary or an intervening stellar or substellar system, with different physical source sizes in each case. We present binary microlensing as a testable interpretation of this event, with the finite-source structure offering a potential probe of the compact GeV-emitting region.

title: Model-Based Retrieval of Four Years of JWST/NIRCam Wavefronts
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, Submitted to PASA
summary: The fidelity of data recovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) depends on precise monitoring of the mirror segments' surfaces and alignment. We typically improve the reduced chi-squared in fits to the defocused data from 60-65 to 12-13. We reconstruct the wavefront history of JWST from the beginning of science operations to early 2026. This open source implementation operates in parallel to the current STScI phase retrieval algorithm, allowing access by the broader scientific community to high-accuracy wavefront estimation and enabling its direct integration into science-analysis workflows. This represents a major step towards the ultimate goal of predictive calibration methods based on physics-based forward modelling, obviating the need for time-consuming observation of contemporaneous dedicated reference stars.

title: Polarization and Burst Properties of the Repeating FRB~20240209A in a Quiescent Elliptical Host
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in ApJ

title: Influence of $Δ$ resonances in hyperonic neutron stars on gravitational-wave inspiral signatures
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D
summary: The composition of dense matter in neutron star interiors remains uncertain, with the possible appearance of the non-strange $Δ$ resonances providing an important source of theoretical uncertainty. We investigate how variations of the scalar and vector $Δ-$meson couplings, subject to \(x_{σΔ}-x_{ωΔ}=0.2\), modify the tidal properties and inspiral gravitational-wave signals. We find that the allowed variation in the $Δ-σ$ coupling leads to substantial changes in the tidal properties of the neutron stars, which in turn leave distinct imprints on the gravitational-wave waveforms, particularly in their frequency evolution, accumulated phase, and strain amplitude. These waveform differences arise through changes in tidal deformability and are not unique signatures of $Δ$ resonances. Future gravitational-wave observations may therefore constrain the $Δ-$meson couplings within the adopted dense-matter framework, subject to degeneracies with alternative EOS models.

title: Measuring Precipitable Water Vapor through Dual-Band GPS at Rubin Observatory
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to PASP
summary: Precipitable water vapor (PWV) in Earth's atmosphere is a known source of systematic error in ground-based astronomical measurements, particularly at wavelengths greater than 7,000 angstroms. PWV produces wavelength-dependent extinction in the spectral energy distributions of observed sources. For high-precision applications, such as supernova cosmology, the transmission function must be measured accurately and precisely for each observation. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is located in the Chilean Andes, a region known for dry conditions. However, even at this location, time-variable absorption by water vapor is a factor. Signal delays from Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) offer a robust, easy, 24-hour monitoring of PWV. In this paper we present measurements from the first six months of GNSS-PWV at Rubin Observatory. We verified our analysis by replicating results from the International GNSS Service (IGS), demonstrating high consistency. We then installed and commissioned a Trimble Net R9 receiver at Allegheny Observatory for a commissioning run before it was relocated to Rubin Observatory. At Rubin Observatory we have been continuously measuring PWV since 2025 September 5. title: The unresolved high-mass frontier of the black hole Fundamental Plane
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for Publications in PASP
summary: Accreting black holes follow a Fundamental Plane (FP) linking radio and X-ray luminosities to black hole mass, but whether this relation changes in the ultramassive regime, above $\sim10^{10}\,\Msun$, remains unresolved.
